content.text: Consciousness is the Self.
Limited knowledge is bondage.
The group of causal sources (the matrix of speech and elements) constitutes the body of ignorance.
The foundation of all limited knowledge is Matrika, the uncomprehended power of sound and letters.
A flash of supreme intuitive awareness (udayama) is Bhairava Himself.
Through union with the wheel of divine energies, the dissolution of the objective universe takes place.
Through the differentiation of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the continuous bliss of Turiya (the fourth state) is experienced.
Common sensory knowledge constitutes the waking state.
Vague conceptual imagination constitutes the dream state.
Lack of discernment and unawareness of reality constitutes deep sleep (sushupti).
He who is the conscious master and consumer of all three states is the lord of heroes (Viresha).
The planes of yogic realization are characterized by supreme wonder (vismaya).
His divine will (iccha-shakti) is Uma, the ever-youthful, immaculate goddess.
All perceptible phenomena are experienced as His own cosmic body.
By unifying the mind in the spiritual heart-center, perception of external forms and inner void dissolves into pure light.
By steadfast focus on the pure transcendental reality (Shuddhatattva), freedom from the bound condition (pashu-shakti) is achieved.
Unshakable, spontaneous conviction of one's divinity is true Self-knowledge.
The pervasive bliss of the world becomes the bliss of his continuous absorption (samadhi).
By contemplation on the supreme divine energy, any desired form or reality can be brought forth.
He masters the union of elements, the dissolution of elements, and the synthesis of the cosmos.
Upon the rise of pure unconditioned knowledge (Shuddhavidya), mastery over the cosmic wheel of energies is attained.
By immersing awareness in the vast lake of cosmic consciousness, the living potency of all sacred mantras is directly realized.
The mind deeply absorbed in the divine essence is itself the mantra.
Zealous, spontaneous effort in awareness is the true practitioner.
The luminous reality of the body of divine knowledge is the secret of all mantras.
The expansion of consciousness within the womb of Maya without full awakening is mere dream-like knowledge.
When pure knowledge spontaneously dawns, the khechari mudra (soaring in the sky of consciousness) reveals the state of Shiva.
The enlightened Guru is the direct means to liberation.
He attains the awakening and illumination of the secret wheel of Matrika.
The yogi's physical body becomes the sacred sacrificial offering in the fire of consciousness.
The objective universe of knowledge becomes his spiritual food.
With the withdrawal of objective knowledge, dream-like appearances arising from it dissolve into stillness.
The individual soul bound in worldly transmigrations identifies itself as the finite mind.
Its attachment to dualistic, fragmented knowledge is its bondage.
Non-discernment of principles such as Kala and Maya creates worldly illusion.
In the physical body, the dissolution of limiting factors (kalas) is to be meditated upon.
The dissolution of pranic nadis, mastery of gross elements, detachment from elements, and separation of components are mastered.
Supernatural powers arise from the veil of spiritual delusion; they are not ultimate freedom.
By conquering delusion and expanding into infinite bliss, mastery of natural, innate wisdom is achieved.
The waking world is experienced merely as a secondary radiance of his own Self.
The Self is the cosmic actor/dancer, performing all roles across the stage of existence.
The inner, subtle soul is the sacred stage upon which the cosmic play unfolds.
The sensory organs are the spectators beholding the divine drama.
By means of refined, illumined intellect, the state of pure sattva is firmly established.
The perfected being achieves absolute, unhindered freedom (svatantrya).
As is his state in divine absorption, so is it in every other circumstance and place.
Owing to the natural radiation of divine consciousness, creation manifests outwardly without diminishing the source.
Steadfast meditation upon the primal seed of consciousness is practiced.
Established in the firm seat of divine awareness, he immerses effortlessly in the lake of immortal nectar.
He creates and manifests according to his own cosmic measure and will.
With the eradication of binding ignorance, rebirth in worldly suffering is permanently destroyed.
In the letters of the alphabet from the ka-group onwards, deities like Maheshvari act as mothers binding the unawakened soul.
Throughout the three states of waking, dreaming, and sleeping, the fourth state (Turiya) should be poured continuously like a stream of oil.
Submerged in his own purified consciousness, he enters the innermost sanctuary of reality.
When the flow of life-breath (prana) becomes harmonized, the vision of cosmic equality dawns.
By resting awareness in the central spiritual channel (sushumna), lower instinctive impulses cease to arise.
By reconnecting fragmented thoughts with the original source, that which was lost is restored to divine life.
He becomes equal to Shiva Himself.
His very bodily life becomes his sacred vow and worship.
His spontaneous, natural speech becomes the recitation of holy mantra (japa).
His gift to the world is the sharing of Self-knowledge.
He who abides unswerving in awareness is the true source of awakening for others.
The manifested universe is recognized as the unfolding play of his own divine energy.
Both the maintenance and dissolution of worldly appearances are within his conscious domain.
Even while actively engaged in worldly affairs, his awareness remains unbroken because he never departs from the knower.
Pleasure and pain are perceived purely as external phenomena, touching not the inner Self.
Freed completely from pleasure, pain, and dualities, he is truly alone and complete (kevali).
He whose awareness is constricted by delusion remains bound to the reactions of karma.
When all distinctions are transcended, the capacity for creating a new spiritual world appears.
The creative power of the senses is experienced directly as an extension of one's own will.
By transcending the three states of experience, omnipresence is fully realized.
For him whose mind is surrendered to divine consciousness, there is no obstruction anywhere in the three worlds.
If one who has ascended to this awareness becomes careless, worldly distraction binds him once again.
For one who remains ever vigilant in divine awareness, no fault or affliction can ever arise.
Filled with unbroken, sovereign bliss, he is Shiva Himself.

content.sanskrit: सर्वज्ञः सर्वकर्त्ता च शिवतुल्यो न संशयः ।
content.transliteration: sarvajñaḥ sarvakarttā ca śivatulyo na saṃśayaḥ |
content.text: Omniscient and all-powerful, he is indistinguishable from Shiva; of this there is no doubt.
Thus conclude the Shiva Sutras of Vasugupta.
